verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to YHWH, for [he is] good, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the LORD! Lift your voices, for he is good, and his faithful love does not end. It reaches to the far edge of time.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the opening call of a liturgy built for two voices. A leader sings the line and the whole congregation answers with the refrain, 'for his covenant loyalty is forever', which recurs in all 26 verses. Stage it that way: the verse is a summons, and the refrain is the crowd answering.

The KJV renders חסד as 'mercy', which makes God sound like a judge who spares the guilty. The word names loyalty inside a bond, the faithfulness that a covenant partner owes and gives. 'Endureth for ever' also adds a verb the Hebrew does not have: the clause is a bare noun phrase, 'to the age his loyalty', and the verb is yours to supply. Hebrew עולם means a distant horizon of time, not an abstract eternity. הודו is more than 'thank': the root ידה means to confess or acknowledge publicly, and the verb is often used for praise spoken aloud before others.

philological_notes.note: Imperative plural of the hiphil of ידה: to acknowledge, confess, give thanks publicly. It is a public act performed before others, not a private feeling.
Covenant loyalty, faithful love: the commitment that holds a relationship together. Metzudat David contrasts it with human חסד, which does not last.

verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to the God of the gods, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the God of gods, to the One above every power that men have named divine. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The phrase 'God of gods' is a Hebrew superlative, in the same family as 'Song of Songs' and 'holy of holies': the God beyond all rivals. Israel sang this among neighbours who had a god for every river, storm and harvest, so this is a quiet claim of rank. The singers do not say the other gods are nothing here; they say they all answer to one.

The KJV 'God of gods' is faithful, but it does not tell a modern reader that the line is a political and religious statement. Ibn Ezra and Radak read 'the gods' as the angels; Malbim reads them as the powers the ancient nations thought ruled the stars. Either way the verse pulls the whole heavenly court under one throne. Play it as a confident aside, not a threat.

philological_notes.note: A construct chain with the same noun twice: the God over all who bear the name god. Radak and Metzudat David take the second 'gods' as angels; Malbim takes them as the powers the nations revered.

verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to the Lord of the lords, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks to the Lord of lords, the Master over every master. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The second step of the climb repeats the first with a different noun: אדון is a master, owner or sovereign, the word a slave used for the one who held him. In a world of kings who took titles like 'king of kings', the singers give that title to YHWH alone. The mood is a rising rhythm, so lean on the doubled noun, 'lord of the lords'.

The KJV 'Lord of lords' is accurate, but its capital L can be confused with the printed 'LORD' that stands for YHWH. Here the Hebrew word is the ordinary title 'adonim', not the divine name, and the verse moves from God's name to God's rank. Ibn Ezra, Radak and Meiri hear angels or the celestial spheres in the 'lords'; Metzudat David hears the host of heaven that was thought to govern the earth.

philological_notes.note: A superlative chain parallel to the preceding verse, with the title 'lord, master'. It is not the divine name; the medieval commentators read 'the lords' as the heavenly bodies or angels that govern the world below.

verses.translation_literal: To the one who does wonders, great ones, to himself alone, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Thank the One who does great wonders, wonders no other hand has ever done. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
From titles the psalm turns to deeds. נפלאות are acts that cut through ordinary expectation, things that make an onlooker stop and stare, and the word is most often used of what God did at the Exodus. The participle 'one who does' is present and ongoing: the wonders are not locked in the past. Hold the pause before 'to himself alone'.

The KJV 'who alone doeth great wonders' puts 'alone' in front of the verb, as if God were the only one active. The Hebrew places it after: לבדו, 'to his own self', the wonders are his without helper. Metzudat David says he needs no help from the angels, and Malbim says he acts without going through the 'gods' and 'lords' of verses 2-3. That is a pointed correction of a world that gave credit for marvels to lesser powers.

philological_notes.note: Niphal participle plural of פלא: things too marvelous to grasp, extraordinary acts. Radak notes it also hints at things the human eye cannot see.
Literally 'to his separateness, by himself'. The noun בַּד means a part or portion; with the suffix, God stands apart from any helper.

verses.translation_literal: To the one who made the heavens by understanding, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Thank the One who made the heavens with understanding, who set the high vault in place with skill. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
Creation begins here, and it is told as craftsmanship. תבונה is skill that discerns and fits parts together, the word the Wisdom tradition uses for how the heavens were framed (compare Proverbs 3:19). The sky is not a fight with a monster, as in the myths of Babylon and Canaan; it is built by a mind. Let the voice slow and grow warm.

The KJV has 'by wisdom', which blurs two Hebrew words. חכמה is wisdom and תבונה is understanding, and Malbim says Scripture assigns the first to the earth and the second to the heavens. The preposition ב matters too: 'by' marks the means. Meiri adds the idea that the heavens were made 'living and wise', but that is his reading, not the plain sense.

philological_notes.note: From בין, to discern: skilled understanding that perceives how parts fit. Malbim distinguishes it from חכמה, which he links to the earth.

verses.translation_literal: To the one who spread out the earth upon the waters, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Thank the One who hammered the earth out flat above the waters. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The ancient picture of the world is a disc of land with water above, below and around it. רקע is a metalworker's verb: to beat out thin, as a smith spreads gold into a sheet. Isaiah 40:19 uses the same root of a goldsmith overlaying an idol, and Metzudat Zion cites that verse. God is imagined as a smith or builder who flattens solid ground out of the waters. The audience would have felt the force of it every time they stood on dry earth.

The KJV 'stretched out ... above the waters' is close, but 'stretched' loses the hammer. The preposition על means 'upon', 'over', 'above'; the psalmist uses it to say that the land rests on, or rises over, the deep. Radak sees a kindness in it: the water naturally wants to cover the earth, and God held it back so that life could live on dry ground.

philological_notes.note: To beat out, hammer flat, spread, as metal is beaten into plate. Metzudat Zion links it to the goldsmith of Isaiah 40:19.

token_glosses.gloss: to the one who spread out

verses.translation_literal: To the one who made great lights, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Thank the One who made the great lights, who hung brightness in the sky. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The word is 'lights', not 'sun and moon'. אורים are light-bearers: the sun, moon and stars that other peoples worshiped as gods. The next two verses name them, but here the psalm withholds the names for a moment, so that the listener sees them first as made things. Let the reader keep the line plain and the pause open before the sun appears.

The KJV rendering 'great lights' is exact and keeps the plural. Genesis 1:16 uses a different word, מאורות, and this psalm's plain אורים is rarer. Ibn Ezra notes that human life depends on the two great lights, and Meiri says they are needed for the world to continue.

philological_notes.note: Plural of אור, light. It is a rare plural, here naming the heavenly lights. Genesis 1 uses the related מְאֹרֹת for the same objects.

verses.translation_literal: [Namely] the sun for rule in the day, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: The sun, set to rule the day. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The sun in this verse is a ruler with a job, not a god. מֶמְשֶׁלֶת is a governor's authority, and it gives the sun an assigned territory: the day. Compare Egypt, where the sun-god Re was king of the gods, and Mesopotamia, where Shamash judged from the sky. In Hebrew, the sun is appointed by YHWH and has a mandate, no more. Note too that the Hebrew has no verb: 'the sun for dominion in the day' hangs on the previous verse's 'who made'.

The object marker אֶת attaches this line to the earlier verb: God made the lights, namely the sun. The KJV 'The sun to rule by day' is fine in sense but drops the preposition ל, 'for', which states the purpose. Metzudat David says God fixed the boundary of the sun's rule, and it does not cross it.

philological_notes.note: From משל, to rule: a governor's authority, 'for dominion'. The sun's authority is delegated and bounded, not independent.

verses.translation_literal: [Namely] the moon and stars for dominions in the night, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: The moon and the stars, set to rule the night. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
Night gets its own governors. The Hebrew uses the plural מֶמְשְׁלוֹת, 'dominions', for the moon and stars together, where the sun had the singular: one sun rules alone, the night has a council of rulers. Mesopotamian tradition called the moon-god Sin and made the stars into divine beings who ruled omens; here the moon and stars are named without titles, as appointed workers.

The KJV 'rule by night' flattens the plural. A shepherd or caravan driver in the desert needed that light, and Radak notes that the travelers in deserts and sailors depend on the moon and stars. Delivered aloud, the verse is a soft counterweight to the bright one before it.

philological_notes.note: Plural of מֶמְשָׁלָה, 'dominions, spheres of rule'. The plural sets the many night-lights against the one sun.

verses.translation_literal: To the one striking Egypt in their firstborn, for to forever [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: To the One who struck Egypt in its firstborn, the heirs of every house. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary: The psalm turns here from creation to history, and the hinge is a blow. The preposition ב in בִּבְכוֹרֵיהֶם marks where the stroke fell: Egypt was struck in its firstborn. Play it as a single hard fact, with no relish and no apology, because the refrain follows it at once and the liturgy wants the congregation to say it in the same breath. A firstborn was the household's heir, its future, and in Egypt the king's own son was counted among them; the tenth plague strikes the point at which a family's continuity and a dynasty's claim to divinity both rest. Radak and Meiri give the plain reason it is singled out: Israel went out by that plague, so the psalmist names the stroke that opened the road. Malbim adds that the very evil that fell on Egypt was turned to Israel's good, bringing them out with a strong hand. Rashi (on Ps 136:10) notes that the text does not say 'their firstborn' as a bare object but 'in their firstborn', and reads the ב as 'by means of': the firstborn rose against their fathers who were holding Israel back, once they heard of the tenth plague from Moses; Metzudat David has the same reading, 'by the hand of their firstborn'. That is a midrashic extension, not the grammar of the verse; the plain sense is the place of the blow. The KJV 'smote Egypt in their firstborn' is accurate, though 'smote' is archaic for the same verb, נכה, used of a deadly blow, and 'mercy' for חֶסֶד softens a covenant word: this is the loyalty of a party bound by oath to the people it is rescuing. Note the shift of pronoun, 'Egypt ... their firstborn', where the country is treated as a singular place and its people as a plural. BBE's 'first-fruits' is a stretch; בְּכוֹר is simply the firstborn son, and the Hebrew gives no hint of the harvest.

philological_notes.note: 'In their firstborn'. The ב marks the place where the blow fell: Egypt was struck in its firstborn. Rashi and Metzudat David read the preposition as 'by means of' / 'by the hand of' the firstborn, a midrashic reading that the firstborn pressed their fathers to release Israel; that is not the plain grammar. The suffix 'their' is plural, agreeing with the people of Egypt, while the noun מִצְרַיִם is the country.

Participle of נָכָה, 'to strike, smite', often with a fatal result. The participle (rather than a finite verb) keeps God as the one whose ongoing character is praised, in line with the other ל-phrases of the psalm.

verses.translation_literal: And he brought Israel out from their midst, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he led Israel out from among them. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse is a quick release after the blow. The grammar changes: the participles of the earlier lines give way to a narrative verb, וַיּוֹצֵא, 'and he brought out', a past event told in sequence. The singers now stop praising and start telling the story of what happened. Here the refrain sounds as relief.

The verb יצא in the hiphil is the standard word of the Exodus, the same as the opening of the Decalogue, 'who brought you out of the land of Egypt'. The KJV 'brought out Israel from among them' is accurate. 'From their midst' (מִתּוֹכָם) is worth hearing: Israel had lived inside Egypt, not beside it, and God extracted them from within. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David say simply 'from within Egypt'. Radak's note that Israel was spared the plagues while living among the Egyptians belongs to the next verse.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil narrative form of יצא: 'and he caused to go out'. The standard verb of the Exodus.
'From their midst': Israel lived inside Egypt and was drawn out from within it.

verses.translation_literal: With a strong hand and with an arm stretched out, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: With a strong hand and an outstretched arm. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
'A strong hand and an outstretched arm' is the stock phrase of Exodus memory, found in Deuteronomy 4:34, 5:15 and 26:8. It borrows the language of Egyptian royal art, where Pharaoh is shown with raised arm smiting enemies. Israel gives the gesture to YHWH, who, not Pharaoh, is the true warrior-king. Stage it with a gesture: the hand clenched, then the arm flung wide.

The KJV has 'stretched out arm', which is fine, and the Hebrew is exactly parallel: 'by a hand strong, and by an arm stretched out'. The participle נטויה is passive: the arm is extended, held out in readiness. Radak treats the phrase as covering all ten plagues, and Metzudat David pictures a hero reaching toward his enemy in battle. Ibn Ezra and Metzudat David add that Israel left 'with a high hand', openly, not as slaves running away.

philological_notes.note: The fixed Exodus formula: a strong hand and an outstretched arm. The arm image is a royal and military gesture. Radak reads it as covering the ten plagues.

verses.translation_literal: To the one cutting the Sea of Reeds into cuttings, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: He took the sea of reeds in his hand and cut it, slice from slice, and the water stood apart in pieces. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalmist does not say the sea 'divided' or 'parted' but uses a butcher's and a surveyor's verb, גָּזַר, 'to cut', and gives it a noun of the same root: the Reed Sea is cut into 'cuttings'. English cannot easily keep the echo; the KJV's 'divided ... into parts' flattens it, and BBE's 'made a way through' drops the cutting altogether. Play the verb hard: this is a sea treated like something carved. The plural also fed an old tradition, in Rashi, Radak and Meiri, that the sea was cut into twelve lanes, one for each tribe, so that no tribe crowded another; Radak and Meiri add that the plain sense may be simply several cuts. Either way, note what the audience heard: a sea was, for Egypt's neighbours, a god or a monster to be slain, and here YHWH slices it with no struggle recorded.

Note also that the KJV's 'Red sea' translates יַם־סוּף, 'sea of reeds', a name for the water, not a colour.

philological_notes.note: A rare noun, 'cut-off pieces', from the same root as the participle 'the one who cuts' just before it. The pair makes a sound play and an image: the sea is cut into pieces. Rashi reads the plural as twelve cuts for twelve tribes.
'Sea of Reeds'. The Greek and then the KJV tradition rendered it 'Red Sea'; the Hebrew names reeds, not colour.

verses.translation_literal: And he made Israel cross in the middle of it, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And through the very heart of it, between the standing walls, he brought Israel across. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is a causative, הֶעֱבִיר: he did not merely let Israel go over, he made them cross, carried them across, as a shepherd leads a flock over a river. The KJV's 'made Israel to pass through' is fair; BBE's 'let Israel go through' weakens the active hand of God. 'In the middle' (תוֹךְ) matters: Ibn Ezra reads it as the people going far in, away from either shore, and Radak stresses that they walked on dry ground, their feet not even wet.

Hear the name 'Israel' as a nation, not a patriarch: the whole company of freed slaves, with children and animals, moving between two cut walls of water. The verb עבר, 'cross', is also the root of 'Hebrew', and the audience would have felt the pun of a people named for crossing.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil, causative: 'and he made cross'. The simple stem is 'to cross, pass over', which is also the root people connect with the name 'Hebrew' (an association, not a proven etymology).
'In the middle of it': Ibn Ezra takes it to show how far from land they went; Radak says they crossed in dry ground at its depth.

verses.translation_literal: And he shook off Pharaoh and his force in the Sea of Reeds, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And then he shook, as a man shakes dust from a garment, and Pharaoh and all his host were flung into the sea of reeds. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
This is the verse the KJV softens most. נִעֵר means 'to shake off, to shake out': the same word is used of shaking out a lap-fold (Neh 5:13); the KJV's 'overthrew' and ASV's 'overthrew' are the general sense, not the image. YLT's 'shook out' is closer. Meiri catches the picture: Pharaoh is like something in the corner of a garment that is shaken out and thrown away. The word also echoes Exodus 14:27, where YHWH 'shakes' Egypt into the sea. Here the greatest king of the age is a crumb on a cloak.

Play the contrast: Pharaoh, god-king, with his chariot corps, the heavy arm of the empire (חַיִל means force, army and also strength), is dismissed with one gesture. Ibn Ezra adds that with Pharaoh gone Israel was truly free.

philological_notes.note: To shake off or out. The word in Exod 14:27, 'YHWH shook off the Egyptians in the midst of the sea', is built from the same root. The image is of shaking something out of cloth or from the hand.
'His force': power, army. The word can mean strength as well as troops, so Pharaoh's army and his strength are shaken off together.

verses.translation_literal: To the one making his people walk in the wilderness, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: He walked his people out into the wilderness, where there is no road and no water and no shade. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verb is again causative, מוֹלִיךְ, 'the one who makes walk': God does not just accompany, he leads, as one leads the flock. The KJV's 'led his people through the wilderness' adds 'through', as though there was an exit in view; the Hebrew has only 'in the wilderness', מִדְבָּר, the empty, unsown land beyond the farm. For an audience of settled farmers, the wilderness was not scenery but the place of thirst, hunger and death.

Radak and Meiri tell you what the tradition heard in the line: the cloud by day and the fire by night, and bread and water from nowhere. Ibn Ezra reads the wilderness as the great one in which Israel followed God. Play it with quiet awe, a long walk in an empty place.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle of 'to walk': 'the one making walk', hence 'leading'. The Hiphil keeps the sense of the hand that guides.
'Wilderness', the unsown steppe beyond the cultivated land; the root connection to 'speak' or 'drive' is debated, so no etymology is built on it here.

verses.translation_literal: To the one striking great kings, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: He struck down kings, great kings, and they fell. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
From wilderness to war. הִכָּה, 'to strike', is the plain verb of blows, softened by the KJV into the biblical-sounding 'smote'; modern English hears 'struck' or 'struck down'. 'Great kings' in the ancient Near East was a title of rank: the great king ruled other, lesser kings, as in Hittite and Assyrian texts. Here the psalm gives the title to the kings Israel met, so that the victory is the larger. Rashi, with a tradition that sees thirty-one kings behind this phrase, and Radak, who notes that the kings refused Israel passage and came out to fight, both describe a strong enemy handed over.

The verse opens a doubling: this line says 'struck', the next says 'killed', and Ibn Ezra and Radak read the pair as one act said twice for emphasis.

philological_notes.note: Hiphil participle: 'the one striking'. The plain word for a blow, used for an enemy being hit down, not necessarily killed; the next verse adds the killing.
'Great kings', a rank word in the ancient Near East for powerful rulers. Rashi treats it as a hint at the thirty-one kings of Canaan, with Sihon weighing against them all.

verses.translation_literal: And he killed mighty kings, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he killed them, the mighty kings, every one. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
Now the blow becomes a death: וַיַּהֲרֹג, 'and he killed'. The KJV's 'slew famous kings' misses twice: 'slew' is archaic, and 'famous' is a poor rendering of אַדִּירִים, which means 'mighty, majestic', the same word used of great waters and of cedars. The psalm raises the stakes with the adjective: first 'great', now 'mighty'. Ibn Ezra quotes the prophet's image of the Amorite who stood tall as the cedars and strong as the oaks (Amos 2:9), the strength that makes the victory worth singing.

A modern audience may flinch at praising God for killing. Do not soften it: the text means it, and it is an old Near Eastern habit to sing the victory of the national god over named kings. Radak notes that the singers go on, in the verses after, to speak of the land as the gift.

philological_notes.note: 'Mighty, majestic'. Used of mighty waters, of the cedar and of nobles; the KJV's 'famous' narrows it to renown, where the word names strength and splendour.
'And he killed': the plain word for killing, harder than the previous 'struck'. Ibn Ezra and Radak take the two verbs as one deed said twice.

verses.translation_literal: To Sihon, king of the Amorite, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Sihon, king of the Amorites, he struck him. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The unnamed kings now get a name. Sihon ruled from Heshbon east of the Jordan, and in Numbers 21 he refused Israel passage and came out against them. The psalm leaves out the verb, which hangs over from verse 18; the line begins with a bare 'to Sihon', as a name given for the roll call. Meiri and Metzudat David remark that the two kings are named separately because of their strength.

The KJV supplies 'Sihon king of the Amorites' with the plural; the Hebrew has the singular collective 'the Amorite', a people spoken of as one man. Read the name slowly: the audience knew these stories and the name alone was enough.

philological_notes.note: 'The Amorite', a singular collective for the people, as is common in Hebrew ('the Canaanite'). English versions make it a plural.

verses.translation_literal: And to Og, king of the Bashan, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And Og, king of Bashan. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The second name, and the last: Og, king of Bashan, the green, well-watered highland north of the Yarmuk, famous for its cattle and its oaks. Numbers 21 and Deuteronomy tell of his defeat, and Og is remembered as a giant, the last of the Rephaim, though the psalm says nothing of that. The Hebrew has 'the Bashan' with the article, a land known as the land, which the KJV's 'Bashan' drops.

The conjunction 'and' at the start of the line makes it a pair with Sihon: the two eastern kings the tradition sets together. Metzudat David notes that Og too is named alone because of his strength. Keep the line short, like a name on a memorial.

philological_notes.note: 'The Bashan', a place name with the article, the highland east of the Jordan. The article marks it as the well-known land.

verses.translation_literal: And he gave their land as an inheritance, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he gave their land, all of it, to be an inheritance. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
After the killing comes the gift, and with it the central word of the psalm's geography: נַחֲלָה, 'inheritance', land that passes within a family from one generation to the next and cannot be sold outright. In an agrarian world, land was the whole of wealth, status and a family's place. 'Gave' (נָתַן) is the verb of grant: Israel does not take the land by right but receives it.

The KJV's 'heritage' is accurate but archaic. Ibn Ezra notes that this land was not part of the covenant territory, which is why the psalm calls it an inheritance; Metzudat David adds that Israel had only asked to pass through. Radak reads it as an extra measure of grace: the land east of the Jordan was beyond what was promised to Abraham.

philological_notes.note: Inherited land held within the family and clan. The word presents the land as gift and as lasting possession.

verses.translation_literal: An inheritance [as] to Israel his servant, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: An inheritance for Israel, his servant. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The verse repeats the last in a new order: נַחֲלָה comes first, and now the receiver is named, 'Israel his servant'. The psalm uses the title עֶבֶד, which is honour as well as subjection: a servant of the great king belongs to his house and is under his care. The KJV's 'Even an heritage' fills in a gap the Hebrew leaves open; the repeated word is a sung echo, the kind of thing a choir takes up.

Radak sets the contrast the hearers would feel: the land is taken from those who served idols and given to the people who serve the one God. Metzudat David adds that the oath to the fathers would have been satisfied with a few righteous ones, but the gift went to all Israel.

philological_notes.note: 'His servant': a title of honour and belonging to the king's household, here applied to the whole people.

verses.translation_literal: Who in our lowliness remembered to us, for to eternity [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: He remembered us when we were brought low. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The voice drops here. After the great conquests of vv.17-22, the congregation speaks about itself, and the word is shefel, the low place, the ground-level condition of a people who are down and cannot rise. The verb is zakhar, 'remembered', and in Hebrew remembering is not recollection but action: God remembers and then something happens (Gen 8:1, Exod 2:24). The preposition is odd to English ears, 'remembered to us', a dative that makes the memory a gift given to us. Play it as relief, spoken quietly.

When does it happen? Readers split. Rashi takes it back to Egypt and quotes Exod 2:24, where God hears the groaning and remembers the covenant. Metzudat David likewise sees Israel at its lowest in Egypt, despised and filthy under crushing labour. Radak and Meiri hear a later exile: Radak says that when Israel was taken out of the land for its sins and lay low in exile, God remembered the covenant of the fathers, and he applies this to the Babylonian exile or another, adding that the latter is the correct reading; Meiri likewise points to Babylon or the present exile. Both read the past tense as a prophetic future, the way prophets speak of what is promised as already done. Malbim goes further: the earlier wonders are a pledge, so that in every low hour the old miracles are remembered for us. The actor can carry all of this without choosing: a people who say 'he remembered' with the certainty of those who have been remembered before.

The KJV's 'low estate' is archaic but faithful, and 'remembered us' smooths the Hebrew dative 'remembered to us'. 'Mercy endureth' is the refrain's chronic softening: chesed is covenant loyalty, a bond with obligations, not a feeling of pity, and l'olam means 'for the age', for as long as time reaches, not a vague 'forever' with a flourish.

philological_notes.note: she- is the short relative particle (later Hebrew), joined to be- 'in', the noun shefel 'low state' and the suffix 'our': 'who in our lowliness'. The noun appears only here and in Eccl 10:6. The relative makes the line a clause that continues the series of 'who ...' acts of God in the psalm.

Remembering in Hebrew is covenant action, not mental recall. The dative 'to us' makes the memory a benefit given to the people, as 'remembered to them his covenant' (Ps 106:45). Rashi on Ps 136:23 sets it in Egypt, citing Exod 2:24.

verses.translation_literal: And he tore us free from our foes, for to the age [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: And he tore us loose from those who pressed us hard. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
פָּרַק is 'to tear off, break away', the word for pulling a yoke or a chain from the neck, and the KJV's 'redeemed' is too churchly and too legal: this is a breaking-loose, not a purchase. The enemies are צָרִים, the ones who 'press' or 'bind in', from the root of 'narrow': the oppressor who leaves no room. Metzudat Zion links the verb to the Aramaic word for rescue, and the Targum renders it with that Aramaic root.

Radak and Meiri note the Hebrew past tense can speak of a future rescue, as prophets often do, so that the line also gives a promise: what he did, he will do. Play the last line of the verse without a flourish. The psalm's refrain has been said twenty-four times; after the tearing free comes the plain, steady sound of it.

philological_notes.note: 'And he tore us free': from a verb for breaking something off, such as a yoke. KJV's 'redeemed' reads a purchase into it. Metzudat Zion ties it to the Aramaic word for deliverance.
'Our foes', literally 'those who press, bind in', from a root of narrowness and distress.

verses.translation_literal: Giving bread to all flesh, for to the age [is] his loyal love.
verses.translation_dramatic: He is the One who gives bread to every living creature, to everything that breathes and hungers. Every mouth that opens finds him already there, and so we say it again: his faithful love does not end, not ever.
verses.directors_commentary:
The psalm has just walked through the exodus, the wilderness and the conquest, the great national story. Here it widens its lens to the whole animate world. "All flesh" (kol-basar) is the same phrase used for every living creature in the flood story, humans and animals alike; the actors should feel the circle drawing out from Israel to the sparrow and the lion cub. The singer is saying that the God of the covenant is also the one who feeds the entire world, a sharp claim in a region where grain, rain and fertility were handed to Baal, Dagan and the Egyptian Nile gods. In a land that lives or dies by the winter rains, "bread" (lechem) means more than loaves: it is food in general, the daily margin between life and famine.

The KJV's "giveth food" is fair, though the Hebrew says lechem, bread, the staple itself, and the participle "giving" is ongoing, not a single past act. Its "mercy" for chesed is the real loss: chesed is loyalty inside a relationship, a commitment kept, not a pitying gesture from above. Notice too that the verse has no "who" or "is": it is a bare participle, "Giving bread," and the refrain answers it like a congregation's response.

philological_notes.note: 'Flesh' as a way of naming everything alive and mortal, humans and animals together. It stresses creaturely need, which is why the next word is bread.
Covenant loyalty, steadfast love: the faithfulness that a party owes within a bond and keeps. English 'mercy' leans toward pardon of an offender and misses the relational sense.

verses.translation_literal: Give thanks to the God of the heavens, for to eternity [is] his covenant loyalty.
verses.translation_dramatic: Give thanks, all of you, to the God of the heavens. His faithful love does not end.
verses.directors_commentary:
The last line is the summons the psalm opened with, hodu, 'give thanks', now addressed upward to the sky. After v.25, where bread goes out to every living thing, the eye lifts from the table to the heavens. Radak draws the link: rain comes from heaven, and rain is the cause of all food, so the God who feeds all flesh is the God of the heavens, whose command sends the rain down in a kindness that never stops. Let the cast turn their faces up on this line.

The title also closes a loop. Verses 2 and 3 began the psalm with 'God of the gods' and 'Lord of the lords', and this final name returns to those titles and crowns them. Meiri hears in it the one God who alone rules over every other god and is higher than every height. In a world where each people assigned its storm, its sun and its sky to a separate deity, to call him 'God of the heavens' is a claim that the rain and the sun belong to him and to no rival. It is quiet polemic, delivered as thanksgiving.

The KJV's 'God of heaven' puts the plural 'heavens' into the singular, and 'O give thanks' pads a plain imperative; the Hebrew is blunt and communal, a plural command. As for the refrain, 'mercy endureth' is the habitual softening: chesed is covenant loyalty. Rashi, who counts twenty-six refrains in the psalm, matches them to the twenty-six generations the world stood before the Torah was given, sustained by that loyalty alone.

philological_notes.note: 'God of the heavens'. In my own observation this exact title occurs only here in the Psalter; later books use the Aramaic-flavoured 'God of heaven' (elohe hashamayim). Placed last, it answers the titles of vv.2-3. Radak reads it as the God whose command sends the rain; Meiri reads it as the one who rules over all gods.
Hiphil imperative plural of yadah: to give thanks, to acknowledge publicly. It is the same word that opens the psalm at v.1, so the poem ends where it began.
